subject: Copywriting
title: De Beers: A Diamond Is Forever
description: A tiny lesson with a big payoff: De Beers: A Diamond Is Forever.

hook.text: Before 1947, diamond engagement rings weren't universal.

buildup.text: Gerety worked at N.W. Ayer. She wrote the line late at night and almost discarded it. The agency nearly rejected it too.

discovery.text: The slogan linked diamonds to eternal love. Returning a diamond became unthinkable—forever means you keep it forever.

twist.text: Diamonds aren't rare. De Beers controlled supply. The slogan manufactured value for an abundant stone through pure copy.

climax.text: AdAge named it the #1 slogan of the 20th century. No other line of copy has generated more industry revenue.

punchline.text: Four words, invented a tradition, built a $72B industry.

details.summary: De Beers' 'A Diamond Is Forever,' written by Frances Gerety in 1947, is considered the greatest advertising slogan of the twentieth century. It single-handedly created the tradition of diamond engagement rings and linked an ordinary mineral to the concept of eternal love.
details.whyItMatters: This slogan reshaped an entire culture's marriage customs and created a multi-billion-dollar market from scratch. It demonstrates the extraordinary power of words to create demand where none existed.
takeaways: Frances Gerety coined the phrase in 1947 for ad agency N.W. Ayer
The slogan discouraged resale by linking diamonds to eternal commitment
De Beers used the slogan for over 70 years without change

faq.question: Did diamond engagement rings exist before the De Beers campaign?
faq.answer: Diamond engagement rings were rare before 1938 when De Beers launched its campaign. Through strategic advertising and celebrity placement, De Beers made diamonds synonymous with love. By 1965, 80% of American brides received diamond rings.

faq.question: Why was 'A Diamond Is Forever' so effective?
faq.answer: The slogan works on multiple levels. It implies diamonds — like love — should never be sold or discarded. This emotional framing also served a business purpose: suppressing the resale market kept diamond prices artificially high.
